generation.hypothesis: Integrating noncollinear spin treatments and beyond‐DFT corrections that explicitly include longitudinal spin fluctuations into spin‐polarized density functional theory (DFT) will enable a more accurate prediction of ferromagnetic ground states in transition-metal based systems.
generation.material_initial_state: A paramagnetic or weakly magnetic transition-metal based compound (e.g., a high-entropy alloy or similar complex alloy) near its magnetic phase transition at low temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace standard spin-polarized DFT with an advanced electronic structure method that incorporates noncollinear spin treatments and many-body (beyond-DFT) corrections alongside explicit longitudinal spin fluctuation (LSF) effects.
generation.conditions: Low temperature (ground state) conditions where thermal fluctuations are minimized, allowing intrinsic magnetic ordering to emerge.
generation.structural_mediator: Subtle exchange interactions and magnetic fluctuations captured through noncollinear spin arrangements and enhanced exchange-correlation treatment.
generation.mechanism: By accounting for noncollinear magnetism and including explicit longitudinal spin fluctuations, the method can capture the many-body quantum effects and subtle exchange interactions that stabilize the ferromagnetic alignment, which standard DFT often underestimates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The refined computational framework will predict a robust ferromagnetic ground state with emergent magnetic moments that agree more closely with experimental data compared to conventional DFT predictions.
generation.baseline: Standard spin-polarized DFT without LSF or noncollinear corrections, which can fail to capture subtle emergent magnetic order in such systems.
generation.boundary: The proposed method is expected to be most effective for metallic systems with significant exchange interactions; its applicability to strongly correlated or low-dimensional materials remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative predictions (e.g., exact magnetic moment sizes) may be sensitive to the choice of exchange-correlation functional and treatment details; further benchmarking against experimental data is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the advanced computational method to a well-characterized ferromagnetic transition-metal alloy where experimental magnetic moments and ordering are reliably established. Compare the computed magnetic properties (e.g., magnetic moments and Curie temperature) with experimental measurements under cryogenic conditions.
measurements: Spin ordering (from neutron scattering or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced method fails to predict ferromagnetic ordering in a system known to be ferromagnetic, or if there is a significant quantitative discrepancy between predicted and measured magnetic moments (beyond accepted uncertainty thresholds), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

decision.trend: Early studies of high‐entropy alloys and related magnetic materials mainly relied on conventional spin‐polarized density functional theory (DFT) to assess magnetic properties. Soon it was recognized that such methods often failed to capture the subtle exchange interactions and magnetic fluctuations needed to reliably distinguish a ferromagnetic ground state from competing magnetic orders. This led to the incorporation of longitudinal spin fluctuation (LSF) treatments (as in the work on the Cantor alloy) within DFT frameworks. These advancements improved the prediction of magnetic moments even when standard calculations predicted zero moments for some elements. However, even with LSF, reliably establishing the presence of a ferromagnetic ground state at low temperatures remains challenging since the treatment of quantum fluctuations and noncollinear spin interactions is still limited.
decision.unsolved: A primary gap is the lack of a fully predictive computational framework that not only captures the subtle exchange interactions at the ground state but also distinguishes ferromagnetic ordering from other competing magnetic states under conditions of low thermal fluctuation.
decision.lever: Integrate noncollinear spin treatment and beyond-DFT corrections (e.g., advanced exchange-correlation functionals or dynamical mean-field theory) into spin-polarized DFT frameworks with explicit treatment of spin fluctuations.
decision.why: Because the trend has been from standard DFT toward incorporating longitudinal spin fluctuations to capture emergent magnetic moments, the next plausible advancement is to further refine these computational methods. By accounting for noncollinear magnetism and many-body correlation effects, the new approach would more accurately capture subtle exchange interactions and reliably predict a ferromagnetic ground state, directly addressing the identified gap.
